AU.text: Australians ring in the New Year 11 hours before London, in the middle of summer heat. The celebration centers on Sydney Harbour, with one of the most famous fireworks displays in the world.

traditions.title: Fireworks over the harbour
traditions.text: Sydney Harbour has two fireworks shows: a family one at 9:00 PM and the main one at midnight over the Harbour Bridge and the Opera House.

traditions.title: New Year in midsummer
traditions.text: January is summer in Australia, so people celebrate at the beach, at barbecues and at picnics outdoors.

traditions.title: A spot with a view
traditions.text: The best spots by the water are claimed well ahead, even during the day: families arrive with blankets and baskets, and many watch from boats.

BR.text: Brazilians call New Year’s Eve Réveillon. In Rio it’s impressive in scale: millions gather on Copacabana, the music plays, and the fireworks reflect off the ocean.

traditions.title: All in white
traditions.text: Brazilians dress in white, the color of peace and purity, and head to the beach, most of all Copacabana.

traditions.title: Seven waves
traditions.text: At midnight people on the shore jump over seven waves, making a wish for each one.

traditions.title: Flowers for Iemanjá
traditions.text: Many people throw flowers into the water as a gift to Iemanjá, goddess of the sea, and ask for happiness in the new year.

FR.text: The French call this night Saint-Sylvestre. It’s a long dinner with loved ones, a kiss at midnight and a stroll through festive Paris, where the Eiffel Tower sparkles.

traditions.title: Réveillon
traditions.text: A long festive dinner with champagne, oysters and foie gras that lasts well into the night.

traditions.title: A kiss under the mistletoe
traditions.text: At midnight, by tradition, people kiss under a sprig of mistletoe for luck in the new year. The old wish “Au gui l’an neuf!” is tied to mistletoe, too.

traditions.title: The Champs-Élysées
traditions.text: Parisians and visitors gather by the Arc de Triomphe: a light show on its walls, a shared countdown and fireworks at midnight.

GB.text: In Britain, New Year means both Scottish Hogmanay and the London fireworks over the Thames. What matters most are hugs, a song at twelve and the first guest through the door.

traditions.title: The bells of Big Ben
traditions.text: At midnight Big Ben strikes twelve, and the main fireworks begin over the Thames, by the London Eye.

traditions.title: Auld Lang Syne
traditions.text: At twelve, people form a circle, join hands and sing the old Scottish song with words by Robert Burns, crossing their arms on the last verse.

traditions.title: The first guest
traditions.text: In Scotland and northern England, people believe that whoever first crosses the threshold after midnight brings luck to the house. They arrive with a gift: coal, shortbread or whisky.

JP.text: For the Japanese, New Year is the most important holiday of the year: quiet, a clean home, temple bells and a family dinner. People welcome midnight at home or at a temple.

traditions.title: Joya no Kane
traditions.text: On New Year’s Eve, Buddhist temples ring their bells 108 times, once for each of the earthly desires a person is cleansed of. The last strike usually rings out in the new year.

traditions.title: Toshikoshi soba
traditions.text: In the evening people eat toshikoshi soba, buckwheat noodles: the long noodles stand for a long life, and how easily they break stands for parting with the troubles of the old year.

traditions.title: Hatsumode
traditions.text: In the first days of January people visit a shrine or temple, the first visit of the year, to pray for a good year and buy a charm.

NZ.text: New Zealand greets the world’s New Year among the first: midnight arrives earlier only on the Line Islands of Kiribati and on New Zealand’s own Chatham Islands.

traditions.title: Fireworks from the Sky Tower
traditions.text: At midnight the fireworks are launched right from the Sky Tower in Auckland, and they can be seen across the whole harbour.

traditions.title: Among the first in the world
traditions.text: Auckland rings in the New Year two hours before Sydney.

traditions.title: Summer holidays
traditions.text: Early January falls in the summer break: families head to beaches and campsites and welcome the night outdoors.

US.text: In the US the main symbol of the night is the New York ball. The country spans six time zones, so from midnight in New York to midnight in Hawaii is five hours.

traditions.title: The Times Square ball
traditions.text: In New York, a minute before midnight a crystal ball begins to descend, and the whole square counts down the last sixty seconds.

traditions.title: A kiss at midnight
traditions.text: By tradition, with the first stroke of twelve you kiss the person closest to you, for luck and love in the new year.

traditions.title: Beans for luck
traditions.text: In the South, people eat black-eyed peas and greens on January 1 for abundance and money.
